unit.unitOverview: This unit teaches the register of careful claims. Environmental and scientific writing is full of hedges, causal chains and citations, and all three exist for the same reason: the claims are probabilistic, the causes are indirect, and the evidence belongs to somebody else. Learning to read that register tells you how confident a writer actually is. Learning to write it lets you make claims you can defend.
unit.learningPath:
Read and listen to the Lesson. There are three patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 2 is the one where correlation and cause get confused.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a research summary and a news report of it.
Do the Practice. Practice 2 is the diagnostic — does this claim cause or correlation?
Record yourself making four hedged claims with sources.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
This unit is about a register rather than a subject. Environmental and scientific writing has three habits, and all three exist for the same reason: the claims are probabilistic, the causes are indirect, and the evidence usually belongs to somebody else.
First pattern: hedging a claim.
In Unit 7 you learned hedges for opinions and disagreements — I tend to think, I am not sure that. This is the same mechanism applied to evidence, and it works in three ways.
Hedging the strength. Tends to, is likely to, appears to, suggests, indicates, is associated with.
Emissions in this sector tend to peak in winter.
The data suggests a link rather than the data proves a link.
Hedging the quantity. Approximately, around, in the region of, up to, broadly.
Approximately forty per cent. Around a fifth. Up to three degrees.
And hedging the scope. In most cases, generally, typically, under these conditions, in this sample.
The last of those matters more than it looks. In this sample tells you the finding may not extend beyond what was measured, and it is one of the most honest phrases in the whole register.
Now the important thing, which is the reverse of what people assume. In careful writing, a hedge is not weakness. It is a claim about your own certainty, and it is itself a piece of information. A writer who says tends to and a writer who says always are telling you two different things about their evidence, and the first is usually the more trustworthy.
The practical consequence is that unhedged claims about complex systems should make you more suspicious, not less. Renewable energy is cheaper is a sentence that has left something out. Renewable energy is now cheaper than gas in most markets, on a levelised cost basis, is a claim somebody could check.
Second pattern: cause and effect, and this is the one that goes wrong.
English has a large vocabulary for causal chains, and it is worth having because environmental claims are almost never single-step.
Leads to. Results in. Gives rise to. Contributes to. Is caused by. Stems from. Is driven by.
And for chains: A leads to B, which in turn results in C.
Now the distinctions that matter.
Contributes to is much weaker than causes. Deforestation contributes to flooding says it is one factor among several. Deforestation causes flooding says it is the cause. Those are different claims and the first is usually the defensible one.
Is associated with is weaker still, and it is doing something specific: it says two things occur together and stops short of saying one produced the other.
Which brings us to the central distinction of this card.
Correlation is not cause. Two things moving together does not tell you that one moved the other.
There are three possibilities every time you see two things correlated. A caused B. B caused A. Or something else caused both.
That third one is the one people forget, and it is often the answer. Ice cream sales and drownings rise together. Neither causes the other; hot weather causes both.
So when you read a claim that two things are linked, the question is not is it true. It is which of the three, and does the writer say?
And there is a wording tell. Careful writers use is associated with, is linked to, correlates with when they mean correlation, and reserve causes, drives, leads to for when they have grounds to claim direction. When a report uses causal language for correlational evidence, that is a real error, and it is the commonest one in reporting of research.
Third pattern: citing a source.
The basic structures: according to, research suggests, a study found, the report concludes, figures published by.
According to is the workhorse and it does something specific: it attributes without endorsing. According to the company's own figures tells the reader whose claim this is and quietly signals that you are not vouching for it.
But here is the point of this card, and it connects directly to Unit 16.
Research suggests is one of the weakest citations available, and it sounds like one of the strongest.
Which research? By whom? How many people or sites? Published where? Funded by whom?
A study found is barely better. One study is one study, and single findings in most fields are provisional until somebody repeats them.
The strong version names things. A 2023 study of four hundred households in three regions, published in a peer-reviewed journal, found that. That is longer and every additional element is something you could check.
So there is a ladder here, exactly as in Unit 16.
Strongest: a named study, with a date, a size and a place of publication.
Then: a named organisation's published figures.
Then: a named report without detail.
Then: research suggests.
Weakest: it has been shown that — which cites nothing at all.
And one last thing about scale, because environmental writing is full of numbers designed to impress. A percentage without a baseline is not information. Emissions fell by 40 per cent means nothing until you know from what, over what period, and measured how. A large percentage of a small number is a small number.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: A Hedge Is Information
readings.passageScript:
Scientific and environmental writing is full of hedges, and learners often read them as weakness or evasion. They are neither. A hedge is a claim about the writer's own certainty, and it is itself a piece of information.
There are three kinds and they hedge different things.
Strength. Tends to, is likely to, appears to, suggests, indicates, is associated with. The data suggests a link is a different claim from the data proves a link, and the difference is not politeness.
Quantity. Approximately, around, in the region of, up to, broadly. Approximately a third is often more honest than 34.2 per cent, because the false precision of the second implies a measurement accuracy that may not exist.
Scope. In most cases, typically, under these conditions, in this sample. That last one matters more than it looks. In this sample tells you the finding may not extend beyond what was actually measured, and it is one of the most honest phrases in the whole register.
Now the consequence, and it reverses what most people assume.
An unhedged claim about a complex system should make you more suspicious, not less.
Renewable energy is cheaper. Cheaper than what, where, measured how, including what costs?
Renewable energy is now cheaper than gas in most markets, on a levelised cost basis. That is longer, more hedged, and checkable.
The first sounds more confident and contains less. The second tells you the basis of comparison, which is where the entire argument lives.
So when you read, notice the hedges and notice their absence. A report that hedges its minor claims and states its central one flatly has told you something about that central claim.
And when you write, hedge honestly. If your evidence is one sample, say in this sample. If your figure is approximate, say approximately. Overclaiming is the fastest way to lose a reader who knows the subject, and a hedge costs one word.

readings.title: Three Possibilities, Not One
readings.passageScript:
Two things move together. What follows?
Three possibilities, always.
A caused B. B caused A. Or something else caused both.
The third is the one people forget and it is frequently the answer.
Ice cream sales and drownings rise and fall together across the year. Neither causes the other; hot weather causes both. The correlation is real, strong, and tells you nothing about ice cream.
So when a report says two things are linked, the useful question is not whether the link exists. It is which of the three, and whether the writer says.
English has a vocabulary that marks this, and careful writers use it precisely.
For correlation: is associated with, is linked to, correlates with, is accompanied by. These say the two occur together and stop there.
For causation: causes, drives, produces, leads to, results in, gives rise to. These claim direction.
And in between: contributes to, is a factor in, plays a part in. These claim direction and deny sole responsibility, which is usually the honest position for anything environmental.
Contributes to is much weaker than causes and it is the word most often needed. Deforestation contributes to flooding is defensible. Deforestation causes flooding is not, because flooding has several causes and the claim as written excludes them.
The commonest failure in reporting research is using causal language for correlational evidence. A study finds an association; the report of it says causes. Nothing was fabricated and the claim changed completely.
There is one more move worth knowing, because environmental claims are rarely single-step. Chains are built with which in turn, and thereby.
Warmer winters reduce frost, which in turn allows the species to overwinter further north, thereby extending its range.
Three steps, each marked. And each step is a place where the chain can break, which is why writing it out in full is more honest than the one-sentence version that jumps from the first cause to the last effect.

readings.passageScript:
STUDY SUMMARY - as published

  We measured nitrate concentrations at 34
  monitoring points across three river
  catchments between 2019 and 2023.

  Concentrations were approximately 18 per
  cent lower at the end of the period than
  at the start, measured against a 2019
  baseline.

  The reduction was associated with the
  introduction of buffer strips on
  adjacent farmland, which occurred over
  the same period.

  We note that rainfall in 2022 and 2023
  was below the twenty-year average, which
  may independently reduce measured
  concentrations. We were unable to
  separate the two effects.

  These findings apply to this sample and
  should be treated as tentative.

-----------------------------------------

  NEWS REPORT - the following day

  BUFFER STRIPS CUT RIVER POLLUTION BY A
  FIFTH

  New research has shown that buffer
  strips on farmland reduce nitrate
  pollution in rivers by almost 20 per
  cent.

  The study, which monitored rivers over
  four years, proves that the measure
  works and campaigners have called for it
  to be made compulsory nationwide.

  Research suggests similar gains could be
  achieved across the country.

grammar.title: Hedging a claim
grammar.explanation: The same mechanism as Unit 7, applied to evidence rather than to opinion. Three kinds, and a hedge is information rather than weakness.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
STRENGTH
  tends to, is likely to, appears to,
  suggests, indicates, is associated with
     The data SUGGESTS a link. (not proves)

QUANTITY
  approximately, around, up to, broadly
     approximately a third
  ^ often MORE honest than 34.2 per cent,
    which implies precision that may not
    exist.

SCOPE
  in most cases, typically, generally,
  under these conditions, IN THIS SAMPLE
  ^ the most honest phrase in the register.

A HEDGE IS INFORMATION
  it is a claim about your CERTAINTY.
  "tends to" and "always" tell the reader
  two different things about your evidence.

THE CONSEQUENCE
  an UNHEDGED claim about a complex system
  should make you MORE suspicious.

     "Renewable energy is cheaper."
     cheaper than what, where, how measured?

     "...cheaper than gas in most markets,
      on a levelised cost basis."
     longer, hedged, CHECKABLE.
grammar.workedExample:
You have measured something at 34 sites and found an 18 per cent reduction.
1. Hedge the quantity. Was it exactly 18? It was approximately 18, so say approximately.
2. Hedge the strength. Do you know the reduction was caused by what you think caused it? If you only know they happened together, use was associated with rather than was caused by.
3. Hedge the scope. Did you measure the whole country, or 34 points in three catchments? Say these findings apply to this sample.
Result: concentrations were approximately 18 per cent lower, and the reduction was associated with the introduction of buffer strips over the same period. These findings apply to this sample.
Three hedges, and every one of them is a true statement about what you actually know.
Now the reading side. You see: buffer strips cut river pollution by a fifth. No hedge on strength, none on quantity, none on scope. Every one of those absences is a claim, and the writer may not have the evidence for any of them.
grammar.commonMistake: Reading hedges as weakness and removing them to sound more confident. The result is a claim you cannot defend, and any reader who knows the subject will discount everything else you say. The opposite error is hedging everything indiscriminately, which — as in Unit 7 — makes it impossible to tell what you actually found.
grammar.memoryTip: Hedge strength, quantity and scope. An unhedged claim about a complex system is a warning.
grammar.practice:
Hedge each claim appropriately, and say which kind of hedge you used.
1. Emissions fell by 18 per cent.
2. Buffer strips reduce nitrate pollution.
3. This applies across the country.
4. Renewable energy is cheaper.
5. Habitat loss is the main driver.
6. The two studies agree.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Emissions fell by approximately 18 per cent. — quantity
2. Buffer strips are associated with reduced nitrate concentrations. — strength
3. These findings apply to this sample. — scope
4. Renewable energy is now cheaper than gas in most markets, on a levelised cost basis. — strength and scope, plus a stated basis of comparison
5. Habitat loss appears to be the main driver. — strength
6. The two studies broadly agree. — strength
Number 4 needed most work, because the original hedged nothing at all and also omitted the basis of comparison — which is where the whole argument lives.
Number 2 is the important one. Changing reduce to is associated with changes a causal claim into a correlational one, and only the second is supported by measuring two things happening at the same time.

grammar.title: Cause, correlation and chains
grammar.explanation: Two things moving together has three possible explanations, and English has vocabulary that marks which one you are claiming. Using the wrong one is the commonest error in reporting research.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
TWO THINGS MOVE TOGETHER.
THREE POSSIBILITIES, ALWAYS:
   A caused B
   B caused A
   SOMETHING ELSE caused both

  ^ the third is forgotten, and it is
    often the answer. Ice cream sales and
    drownings rise together. Hot weather
    causes both.

THE VOCABULARY MARKS YOUR CLAIM

  CORRELATION only
     is associated with, is linked to,
     correlates with

  CAUSATION
     causes, drives, leads to, results in

  IN BETWEEN - one factor among several
     contributes to, is a factor in

  CONTRIBUTES TO is usually the honest one.
     "Deforestation contributes to
      flooding" - defensible.
     "...causes flooding" - excludes the
      other causes.

CHAINS: which in turn, thereby
  Warmer winters reduce frost, which in
  turn allows the species to overwinter
  further north, thereby extending its
  range.
grammar.workedExample:
You have measured nitrate levels falling at the same time as buffer strips were introduced.
1. What do you actually know? That both things happened over the same period.
2. Apply the three possibilities. Did the strips reduce the nitrate? Possibly. Did the nitrate reduction cause the strips? No, that makes no sense here. Did something else cause both? Rainfall was below average in the same years, and low rainfall independently reduces measured concentrations.
3. So the third possibility is live and you cannot rule it out.
4. That means correlational vocabulary: the reduction was associated with the introduction of buffer strips.
5. If you wrote buffer strips reduced nitrate concentrations, you would have claimed direction you cannot support.
Now a chain. You want to say that warmer winters are extending a species' range.
1. Write the steps: warmer winters, less frost, survival further north, wider range.
2. Mark each: Warmer winters reduce frost, which in turn allows the species to overwinter further north, thereby extending its range.
Three steps, three places the chain could break, all visible to the reader.
grammar.commonMistake: Using causal verbs for correlational evidence — writing reduces when your data shows only that two things happened together. It is the commonest error in reporting research and nothing has to be fabricated to produce it. The other error is forgetting the third possibility: two things can correlate because a third thing drives both, and that explanation is often the correct one.
grammar.memoryTip: Associated with for correlation. Contributes to for one factor. Causes only with grounds.
grammar.practice:
Choose the right verb and say why.
1. Two things happen together; you cannot rule out a third factor.
2. Deforestation is one of several causes of flooding.
3. You have experimental grounds for claiming direction.
4. A drought makes an existing shortage worse.
5. Efficiency gains are cancelled out by rising demand.
6. Write a three-step chain about warmer winters and a species' range.
grammar.answerKey:
1. is associated with — you know they occur together and nothing more.
2. contributes to — one factor among several, which is the defensible claim.
3. causes, or leads to — direction is supported.
4. exacerbates — the problem existed first, which is precisely what exacerbate means.
5. are offset by — the effects cancel, and the total may be unchanged.
6. Model: Warmer winters reduce frost, which in turn allows the species to overwinter further north, thereby extending its range.
Numbers 1, 2 and 3 are the three positions on the scale, and choosing between them is a claim about your evidence rather than about your subject.
Number 4 is worth noticing: exacerbate carries a built-in assumption that the problem pre-existed. If it did not, the word is wrong.

grammar.title: Citing a source
grammar.explanation: The structures for attributing evidence, and a ladder like the one in Unit 16 — because the weakest citation in this register sounds like one of the strongest.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE STRUCTURES
  according to...   research suggests...
  a study found...  figures published by...

ACCORDING TO attributes WITHOUT endorsing
  "According to the company's own figures"

THE LADDER
  1 a named study: date, size, publication
  2 a named organisation's published figures
  3 a named report, no detail
  4 "research suggests"
  5 "it has been shown that" - cites nothing

  RESEARCH SUGGESTS sounds strong and
  cites almost nothing.
     Which research? By whom? How many?
     Published where? Funded by whom?

  A STUDY FOUND is barely better.
  One study is one study.

NUMBERS NEED A BASELINE
  "Emissions fell 40 per cent"
  from WHAT, over WHAT period,
  measured HOW?
  A large percentage of a small number
  is a small number.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to cite a piece of research supporting a claim.
1. The weak version: research suggests buffer strips reduce nitrate pollution.
2. Apply the questions. Which research? How large? Published where? None of it is there.
3. Build the strong version by adding what you know: a 2023 study measuring nitrate at 34 points across three catchments over four years found concentrations approximately 18 per cent lower against a 2019 baseline.
4. Every element added — the year, the number of points, the number of catchments, the period, the baseline — is something a reader could check.
5. Note that the strong version also became more hedged, because naming the details forces you to state what was actually measured.
Now the baseline point. Emissions fell by 40 per cent.
1. From what? Against which year?
2. Over what period? A 40 per cent fall over thirty years and over three years are very different claims.
3. Measured how — total, or per unit of output? Those can move in opposite directions.
Without those three, the number is not information.
grammar.commonMistake: Using research suggests as though it were strong support. It sounds authoritative and cites nothing, and it is the phrase most commonly used to carry the broadest claim in a piece. The other error is quoting a percentage with no baseline — emissions fell by 40 per cent is not a fact until you know from what, over what period and measured how.
grammar.memoryTip: Name the study, the size and the date. A percentage with no baseline is not information.
grammar.practice:
Rank each from 1 to 5 and say what is missing.
1. Research suggests the measure works.
2. A 2023 study of 34 monitoring points across three catchments found an 18 per cent reduction against a 2019 baseline.
3. According to figures published by the agency, concentrations fell.
4. It has been shown that buffer strips are effective.
5. A recent report concluded that the measure works.
6. Emissions fell by 40 per cent.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Level 4 — which research, how large, published where.
2. Level 1 — nothing missing. Date, size, location, period and baseline are all present.
3. Level 2 — a named organisation's published figures; missing the size of the fall and the period.
4. Level 5 — cites nothing at all. Shown by whom?
5. Level 3 — a report is named as existing but not identified; missing its author, date and method.
6. Not a citation problem but a baseline problem — from what, over what period, and measured how. Without those three it is not information.
Number 2 is longer than all the others and every extra word is checkable, which is the whole argument of this card.
Number 6 is worth remembering separately: a large percentage of a small number is a small number, and a fall of 40 per cent over thirty years is a very different claim from the same fall over three.

writing.title: Writing 1 — A finding, written properly
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Take something you have observed or measured — at work, in a study, in daily life. It may be small.
Write it up in six to eight sentences as a careful finding.
State what you measured and over what period.
Hedge the quantity.
Use the causal vocabulary that matches your evidence, and no stronger.
Name at least one thing you could not rule out.
State the scope explicitly.
Then write two lines: which verb you were tempted to use and did not, and what a reader could check.
writing.modelText:
Between January and June I recorded how long booking-in took on our bay, on twenty-two days chosen because I happened to be on shift.
The average was approximately fourteen minutes, against approximately twenty-two minutes when I began recording in January.
The reduction was associated with the change to a single-entry screen, which was introduced in March over the same period.
I could not rule out two other factors. Volumes were lower in May and June than in the spring, and two experienced staff joined the bay in April. Either could independently reduce the time taken.
These figures come from one bay and from days when I was present, which are not a random sample of days.
The finding is tentative and would need a fuller record to confirm.

1. I was tempted to write the new screen cut booking-in time by a third. I wrote was associated with, because I measured two things happening together and did not test either alone.
2. A reader could check the dates of the screen change, the volume figures for each month, the staffing dates, and the twenty-two days I recorded.
writing.expectedLength: Six to eight sentences plus two lines
writing.successCriteria: States what was measured and the period; hedges the quantity; uses causal vocabulary matching the evidence; names at least one confounding factor that could not be ruled out; states the scope explicitly; two lines identifying the tempting stronger verb and what a reader could check
writing.support: Write the confounding factors before you write the finding. If you cannot name one, you have probably not thought about the third possibility, and it is nearly always there.
writing.extension: Rewrite it as a headline. Notice how many of the hedges the headline cannot carry, and which one you would most regret losing.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Study into report
writing.promptAndInstructions:

writing.modelText:
RIVER NITRATE FALLS WHERE BUFFER STRIPS ADDED, BUT RAINFALL CLOUDS PICTURE

Nitrate concentrations in three river catchments were around 18 per cent lower in 2023 than in 2019, according to a study of 34 monitoring points published this week.

The fall coincided with the introduction of buffer strips on neighbouring farmland over the same four years. The authors say the two are associated but stop short of concluding that the strips caused the reduction.

Rainfall in 2022 and 2023 was below the twenty-year average, which can itself lower measured concentrations, and the researchers were unable to separate the two effects.

The study covers three catchments and its authors describe the findings as tentative. Whether similar reductions would follow elsewhere has not been tested.

1. The hardest thing to keep was the confounding factor, because it makes the story much less clean and it belongs in the third paragraph rather than the last.
2. The headline had to give up the causal claim. Buffer strips cut pollution is a headline; where buffer strips were added, nitrate fell is barely one.
3. It is less dramatic and I do not think it is less interesting. The rainfall problem is the most interesting thing in the study, and the report in Reading 3 leaves it out entirely.

writing.support: Write the headline last. Writing it first pulls the whole piece towards a causal claim, which is precisely how the version in Reading 3 came about.
writing.extension: Count the hedges in your version and in Reading 3's. Then count the words. Yours will be longer and the difference is smaller than you expect.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the study and the report
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Use the study summary and the news report in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. What does the study claim about the relationship, and what does the report claim?
2. What confounding factor does the study name, and what does the report do with it?
3. The study says its findings apply to this sample and are tentative. What happens to that in the report?
4. The report says research suggests similar gains could be achieved nationwide. Which research?

writing.modelText:
1. The study says the reduction was associated with the introduction of buffer strips — a correlation, with no claim about direction. The report says the strips reduce pollution and that the study proves the measure works, which are causal claims the study explicitly declines to make.
2. Rainfall in 2022 and 2023 was below the twenty-year average, which may independently reduce measured concentrations, and the authors state they could not separate the two effects. The report does not mention it at all.
3. Both are dropped. The report gives no indication that the study covered three catchments, and it converts a tentative finding into a proof.
4. None is named. The only research described is the study itself, which says the opposite — that its findings apply to its own sample. The phrase cites nothing and carries the report's broadest claim.
5. It misrepresents by removal and by verb choice rather than by invention. Every number in it comes from the study. What changed is that associated with became reduce and proves, the confounding factor was deleted, and the scope limitation was replaced by a national claim. A reader of the report would believe something the study takes care not to assert.

writing.support: Put the two texts side by side and underline every verb that describes the relationship. The study has one — associated with. The report has two — reduce and proves. That underlining answers most of question 1 and all of question 5.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Cause, correlation or one factor?
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Choose the right verb phrase and say which of the three possibilities applies.
1. Two things happen together and a third factor cannot be ruled out.
2. Deforestation is one of several causes of flooding.
3. There are experimental grounds for claiming direction.
4. A drought makes an existing shortage worse.
5. Efficiency gains are cancelled by rising demand.
6. Ice cream sales and drownings rise together in summer.
7. Warming makes an existing decline faster.
8. A measure reduces a symptom without addressing the cause.
9. Nothing in a plan works against a rising trend.
10. A change is one of about five things that reduced the figure.
11. A study measures two things over the same period.
12. A controlled trial shows the treatment works.
activities.answerSummary:
1. is associated with — you know only that they co-occur.
2. contributes to — one factor among several.
3. causes or leads to — direction supported.
4. exacerbates — the problem pre-existed.
5. are offset by — the effects cancel.
6. are associated with; hot weather is the likely cause of both — the third possibility.
7. accelerates — it speeds an existing trend rather than starting it.
8. alleviates — it reduces the symptom, not the cause.
9. counteracts — nothing in the plan counteracts it.
10. contributes to — one of several.
11. is associated with — measurement over the same period is not a test of direction.
12. causes — a controlled trial is what licenses the causal verb.
Numbers 1, 6 and 11 all describe the same evidential situation and all take correlational vocabulary. Number 6 makes the third possibility explicit, which is what the others should also do where a candidate exists.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Rank the citation
activities.instructionsAndItems:

1. Research suggests the measure works.
2. A 2023 study of 34 monitoring points across three catchments found an 18 per cent reduction against a 2019 baseline.
3. According to figures published by the agency, concentrations fell.

5. A recent report concluded that the measure works.
6. Emissions fell by 40 per cent.
7. Experts agree that the trend is continuing.
8. According to the company's own figures, emissions fell.
9. Scientists have found a link.
10. The government's published data, released in March, shows a 4 per cent fall since 2019.
11. Studies have shown this repeatedly.

2. Level 1 — nothing missing.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Build the chain
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Turn each one-step claim into a chain of at least three steps, using which in turn and thereby. Then name the weakest step.
1. Warmer winters extend the species' range.
2. Deforestation contributes to flooding.
3. Buffer strips are associated with lower nitrate concentrations.
4. Rising demand offsets efficiency gains.
activities.answerSummary:
Model answers.
1. Warmer winters reduce the number of frost days, which in turn allows more individuals to survive the winter at higher latitudes, thereby extending the range northwards. Weakest step: the second, because survival may be limited by something other than frost.
2. Removing tree cover reduces the amount of rainfall intercepted before it reaches the ground, which in turn increases run-off into watercourses, thereby raising peak river levels after heavy rain. Weakest step: the third, because peak levels also depend on channel capacity and on what is downstream.
3. Buffer strips slow surface run-off from fields, which in turn allows more nitrate to be taken up by vegetation before it reaches the watercourse, thereby lowering measured concentrations downstream. Weakest step: the first, because run-off routes vary with soil and slope and the strips may be bypassed entirely.
4. Improved efficiency lowers the cost per unit of output, which in turn makes additional output economically attractive, thereby raising total consumption despite the efficiency gain. Weakest step: the second, because demand may be limited by something other than price.
Every chain has a weakest step and finding it is the point. The one-sentence version of each of these hides three assumptions inside a single verb.
Number 4 is worth noticing: it is a real and well-documented effect, and the chain shows why an efficiency measure can leave total consumption unchanged.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Find a study and its report
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Find a piece of research reported in the news, and find the study summary or abstract it is based on.
Write down: the relationship verb the study uses, and the one the report uses.
Write down any limitation the study states and whether the report mentions it.
Then write two lines on what changed between them.
activities.answerSummary:
No key — it is your study.
What most people find: the verb gets stronger. Associated with becomes linked to becomes causes or reduces, and the change usually happens between the abstract and the headline rather than in the body of the article.
The second finding is about limitations. Almost every study states them, usually in the last paragraph of the abstract, and reports mention them roughly a third of the time. When a limitation is omitted it is nearly always the one that would most weaken the story.
The third finding is worth holding on to. The journalist usually has not fabricated anything, and often has not even read past the press release the institution issued — which is where the strengthening frequently begins. Blaming the reporter is usually the wrong analysis.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Check a percentage
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Find four percentage claims in real writing — news, advertising, a report, a policy document.
For each, write down: the baseline, the period, and how it was measured.
Mark any where one or more of the three is missing.
Then write one line on which claim would change most if you knew all three.
activities.answerSummary:
No key — they are your claims.
What most people find: at least two of the four are missing a baseline entirely, and the baseline is the one most often absent. A percentage change with no starting point is extremely common and reads as information.
The second finding is about periods. Where a period is given it is often chosen, and the choice matters — a fall since a peak year is a different claim from a fall since a typical year, and both may be true of the same data.
The third finding is the useful one: the claim that changes most when you know all three is usually the one that sounded most impressive. A large percentage of a small number is a small number, and doubling from two cases to four is a hundred per cent increase.

The second finding is about limitations. Almost every study states them, usually in the last paragraph of the abstract, and reports mention them roughly a third of the time. When a limitation is omitted it is nearly always the one that would most weaken the story.
The third finding is worth holding on to. The journalist usually has not fabricated anything, and often has not even read past the press release the institution issued — which is where the strengthening frequently begins. Blaming the reporter is usually the wrong analysis.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
No key — they are your claims.
What most people find: at least two of the four are missing a baseline entirely, and the baseline is the one most often absent. A percentage change with no starting point is extremely common and reads as information.
The second finding is about periods. Where a period is given it is often chosen, and the choice matters — a fall since a peak year is a different claim from a fall since a typical year, and both may be true of the same data.
The third finding is the useful one: the claim that changes most when you know all three is usually the one that sounded most impressive. A large percentage of a small number is a small number, and doubling from two cases to four is a hundred per cent increase.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Strength, quantity and scope — They hedge different things, and a writer may hedge one and not the others — which is itself informative about their evidence.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: The false precision implies an accuracy that may not exist — Precision reads as rigour, and unearned precision is a form of overclaiming.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Something has been left out — Renewable energy is cheaper does not say cheaper than what, where, or measured how. The hedged version is longer and checkable.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Three — A caused B, B caused A, or something else caused both. The third is the one people forget and it is frequently the answer.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: is associated with — Correlational evidence takes correlational vocabulary. Using a causal verb for it is the commonest error in reporting research.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Deforestation contributes to flooding. — Contributes to claims direction and denies sole responsibility, which is usually the honest position for anything environmental.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: exacerbates — Exacerbate carries a built-in assumption that the problem existed first. If it did not, the word is wrong.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Near the weakest — it cites nothing checkable — Which research, by whom, how large, published where, funded by whom. It sounds authoritative and answers none of those.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Attributes without endorsing — It tells the reader whose claim it is and quietly signals that the writer is not vouching for it. That is exactly what according to is for.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: The baseline, the period and how it was measured — A large percentage of a small number is a small number, and a 40 per cent fall over thirty years is a very different claim from the same fall over three.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: A correlational claim has become a causal one — Nothing was fabricated and the claim changed completely, which is what makes this failure hard to spot without watching the verbs.
